idiom_name: ownership-declaring base type (or declaration-level copy suppression) + explicit transfer
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the type a single owner and say so in its declaration. Where the language lets the compiler reject copies (deleted copy operations, a noncopyable type modifier, reference semantics), declare the refusal next to the type and close both paths - the copy constructor and the copy-assignment path - because closing one leaves the other open. Where it does not (dynamic languages, C without hidden representation, C# structs), make duplication impossible in practice: hide construction behind a factory, brand instances with an unexported field or handle, and raise from every copy hook the runtime offers. In every language, pair non-copyability with the sanctioned way to relocate ownership - a move/transfer operation, a consuming parameter, or a shared-ownership handle - because a resource that can neither be copied nor passed on is a design dead end.
code_sketch:
type Handle { private state }          # single owner; no copy operation exists
transfer(h: Handle) -> Handle          # the only sanctioned way to hand it on
# copy attempt -> compile/type error, or the guard raises where the runtime cannot check
pitfalls: Suppressing copies without providing transfer forces callers into aliasing hacks; design the hand-off operation first, then remove the copy.
Applying it to value-like types (money, dates, DTOs) breaks value semantics and container use; the test is whether two equal instances are interchangeable.
A hand-written guard that raises converts a build error into a production failure; prefer the language's declaration mechanism whenever one exists.

Wrong move: treat a reference-semantic object as a unique owner -> assigning two references still aliases one resource and can double-close or race -> instead use a move-only handle, or state shared ownership explicitly with reference counting.

Wrong move: delete copy construction and assignment without designing transfer -> callers cannot return or pass the resource and start aliasing or leaking it -> instead define move, consume, or hand-off operations in the same API change.

Wrong move: treat a runtime guard or static-analysis warning as compile-time enforcement -> ignored checks, reflection, or alternate copy hooks can still duplicate the value -> instead use declaration-level support where available and gate weaker checks in CI.
